topic.title: Who your RM works for
topic.claim: The relationship manager who calls you 'sir' and remembers your birthday earns more when you buy the product that's worse for you.
topic.moment: The bank RM visits with a 'guaranteed return' plan that is half insurance, half investment.

turn.believed: The RM is the bank's free advisor for me.
turn.actually: The RM is a salesperson with targets, and some products pay far better commissions than others.

topic.feeling: Naive for trusting the friendliest person at the bank.
topic.villain: Cross-sell targets and commission structures inside banks
topic.because: Insurance-linked plans pay higher commissions than a plain FD or index fund. The warmth is real, and so is the target.
topic.payoff: Ask your RM one question: 'What do you earn if I buy this?' Watch how long the answer takes.
topic.behaviour: RMs push ULIPs and endowment plans to salaried customers and to their parents.
topic.mechanism: The product that pays the seller most gets pitched hardest.
topic.group: Salaried account holders and their parents
topic.send_to: Their parents, who just got a call from the bank
topic.why_now: Bonus and year-end tax-saving season is when the RM calls start.
topic.needs_facts: That commissions on insurance-linked products are higher than on plain deposits, from IRDAI or SEBI disclosures

score.why: The friendly bank RM is a salesperson with a target, and the question 'what do you earn?' is a test readers can run. A natural one to send to parents.

notes: slide 5: "Pay ₹1 lakh in year one, and about ₹27,000 is the bank's commission" reads as if it describes the plan the RM is pitching. The 27% is an average across all life policies. Say "on average" in that line so the sum stays honest. Also replace the stock opener "Here's what the brochure leaves out" with fresher words, e.g. start straight on the number.

slide 8: the IRDAI draft line turns a decoding of the RM's pitch into a mini news recap, and it comes after the 27% and senior-FD facts. Cut it to one plain clause ("even the regulator calls this mis-selling") or drop the ban-on-incentives detail. Keep "It isn't foolishness. Our parents trusted the branch" as the emotional beat.

slide 3: it repeats slide 1 (earns more, target) and partly slide 2. Merge slides 2 and 3 or sharpen 3 into one new beat, e.g. the warmth is how the job gets done. The 'sir', chai and Diwali message are the sales process, not a bonus on top of it. This is also where a sensory detail could go (the branch chai, the call that starts with "Sir, kaise hain?").

slide 9: the test is good, but give it one more beat so it stings. Name what the pause or the "Sir, that's not how it works" deflection tells you, in a short human line. Don't add a lecture and don't write "do this".

cover/slide 1: the headline field still has a bracket placeholder ("[the worse plan]"). Make it a clean line, e.g. "Your bank RM earns more when you buy the worse plan". Make sure the sub-line doesn't hint at the closing question.

mechanism.broken_premise: None of the three premises fails. Two need tightening. (1) The 27% and 62% figures are what banks earn as corporate agents. They are not the RM's own pay. The RM's link to them is the staff incentive scheme, and IRDAI's September 2026 draft would ban volume-linked and reward-linked incentives for bank and NBFC staff selling insurance, which tells you such schemes exist. (2) An FD pays no commission at all. The bank earns the gap between the FD rate and its lending rate, so 'pays the seller far less' is true only in the sense that an FD sale brings far less fee income or incentive than an insurance sale. The bonus and tax-season timing in premise 3 is a generalization about how pitches tend to arrive, not a factual claim to falsify. The ₹27,000-on-₹1 lakh example is the 27% average applied correctly.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Banks sell life policies as corporate agents and are paid by the insurer as a share of the premium. In FY2025 that averaged 27% of the first-year premium (maximum 62%), but only about 10% of total premium, so the money is heavily front-loaded into year one. An FD earns the bank its interest spread rather than a commission, and an index fund bought through a distributor pays only a small yearly trail built into the regular plan's expense ratio, typically around 0.5–1% a year in Indian mutual funds generally and usually less for index funds. IRDAI's 23 September 2026 consultation paper is still a draft. It proposes a 20% first-year and 3% renewal commission cap on long-term life products, bans volume-linked incentives for bank and NBFC staff, and lists 'selling ULIPs to risk-averse or older customers without adequately explaining investment risks and charges' as mis-selling. The draft's wording is 'older', not 'retired'.

sources.fact: IRDAI's September 2026 draft would cap bank-distributor commissions and ban volume-linked incentives for bank staff. Banks earned an average 27% first-year commission on life policies in FY2025, up to 62%, and the draft names selling ULIPs to risk-averse customers as mis-selling.
sources.excerpt: Life (FY2025 actuals, per Kotak): Banks earned an average first-year commission of 27% on life policies, with a maximum of 62%. For individual products with a premium payment term of 10 years or more, the first-year cap for bank distributors falls to 20%, and renewal commission to 3%. In its list of mis-selling illustrations, the draft cites "ULIPs to risk-averse or post-working-age customers." It also cites "non-par sold in lieu of bank deposits."

sources.fact: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the RBI is concerned about complaints of mis-selling by bank relationship managers. The article quotes an RM saying his performance metrics are tied to a monthly target of Ulips sold.
sources.excerpt: "We are indeed concerned about the complaints." "A relationship manager is not a fiduciary; they are ultimately a sales channel, often incentivised to push certain products." "Let's say I have a target to sell 20 Ulips a month." "My performance metrics are linked to that." Many seniors have ended up signing Ulip or mutual fund forms thinking they were just opening FDs.

sources.fact: IRDAI's consultation paper proposes banning volume-linked or reward-linked incentives for bank and NBFC staff selling insurance, and clawing back commission where mis-selling is proved.
sources.excerpt: The consultation paper also proposes tighter measures to curb mis-selling and compulsory bundling of insurance with other financial products. IRDAI proposes "allowing commission claw-backs in cases of mis-selling," and linking each policy to the individual seller. The proposal includes "prohibiting volume-linked or reward-linked incentives for bank and Non-Banking Financial Company staff selling insurance."

_ledger.text:
[cover] Your bank RM earns more when you buy [the worse plan]
The friendliest person at your bank has a sales target.
 

[slide 1] Your bank's RM sends you birthday wishes, and earns more when you pick the worse plan.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] We treat the RM as the bank's free advisor. The one person at the branch who actually calls back.

[slide 3] But an RM is a salesperson with a monthly target. The 'sir', the chai and the Diwali message are all real. So is the target.

[slide 4] The call comes when the bonus lands and HR wants your tax proofs.
"Sir, guaranteed return hai. Tax benefit bhi. FD se better."
It's a ULIP or an endowment plan. Half insurance, half investment, with a big maturity number twenty years away.

[slide 5] Here's what the brochure leaves out. In FY2025, banks earned an average 27% first-year commission on life policies. Some earned up to 62%.
Pay ₹1 lakh in year one, and about ₹27,000 is the bank's commission.

[slide 6] A plain FD or an index fund pays the seller far less.
So the plan that pays the branch best reaches your table first. The warmth doesn't change that. It just makes the form easier to sign.

[slide 7] And the call that matters most isn't yours. It's your parents'.
Retired, careful, sitting on FD money. Many seniors have signed ULIP forms thinking they were just opening an FD.

[slide 8] It isn't foolishness. Our parents trusted the branch through decades of passbooks and pension credits.
Even the regulator sees it. IRDAI's September draft lists ULIPs for risk-averse or retired customers as mis-selling, and would ban volume-linked incentives for bank staff.

[slide 9] Next time, ask your RM one question.
"What do you earn if I buy this?"
Watch how long the answer takes.

[end card] Read it again before you sign anything your RM brings in tax-saving season.
Send to your parents, before the bank calls them with a 'guaranteed return' plan.

[caption] What 'guaranteed return' plan has your bank RM pitched to you or your parents, and what did they call it?

[alt text] An eight-slide text post arguing that bank relationship managers, however warm, are salespeople with targets who earn more from insurance-linked plans like ULIPs and endowment policies than from FDs or index funds. It cites average bank commissions on life policies, notes that seniors have signed ULIP forms thinking they were FDs, mentions IRDAI's draft rules, and ends by suggesting you ask your RM what they earn if you buy.

The bank earns the gap between the FD rate and its lending rate, so 'pays the seller far less' is true only in the sense that an FD sale brings far less fee income or incentive than an insurance sale. The bonus and tax-season timing in premise 3 is a generalization about how pitches tend to arrive, not a factual claim to falsify. The ₹27,000-on-₹1 lakh example is the 27% average applied correctly.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Banks sell life policies as corporate agents and are paid by the insurer as a share of the premium. In FY2025 that averaged 27% of the first-year premium (maximum 62%), but only about 10% of total premium, so the money is heavily front-loaded into year one. An FD earns the bank its interest spread rather than a commission, and an index fund bought through a distributor pays only a small yearly trail built into the regular plan's expense ratio, typically around 0.5–1% a year in Indian mutual funds generally and usually less for index funds. IRDAI's 23 September 2026 consultation paper is still a draft. It proposes a 20% first-year and 3% renewal commission cap on long-term life products, bans volume-linked incentives for bank and NBFC staff, and lists 'selling ULIPs to risk-averse or older customers without adequately explaining investment risks and charges' as mis-selling. The draft's wording is 'older', not 'retired'.

varun.best: The 'sir', the chai and the Diwali message are all real. So is the target.

alt_texts:
Your bank's RM sends you birthday wishes, and earns more when you pick the worse plan.
Swipe to read →
We treat the RM as the bank's free advisor. The one person at the branch who actually calls back.
But an RM is a salesperson with a monthly target. The 'sir', the chai and the Diwali message are all real. So is the target.

The call comes when the bonus lands and HR wants your tax proofs. "Sir, guaranteed return hai. Tax benefit bhi. FD se better." It's a ULIP or an endowment plan. Half insurance, half investment, with a big maturity number twenty years away.

Here's what the brochure leaves out. In FY2025, banks earned an average 27% first-year commission on life policies. Some earned up to 62%. Pay ₹1 lakh in year one, and about ₹27,000 is the bank's commission.
A plain FD or an index fund pays the seller far less. So the plan that pays the branch best reaches your table first. The warmth doesn't change that. It just makes the form easier to sign.
And the call that matters most isn't yours. It's your parents'. Retired, careful, sitting on FD money. Many seniors have signed ULIP forms thinking they were just opening an FD.

It isn't foolishness. Our parents trusted the branch through decades of passbooks and pension credits. Even the regulator sees it. IRDAI's September draft lists ULIPs for risk-averse or retired customers as mis-selling, and would ban volume-linked incentives for bank staff.
Next time, ask your RM one question. "What do you earn if I buy this?" Watch how long the answer takes.
